findings: No try/catch/finally around `await refreshToken(oldToken)` (lines 19-21 of tokenService.js): if `api.post('/auth/refresh', ...)` rejects (network error, 5xx, timeout), the exception propagates up uncaught and `refreshing` is never reset to `false`. Every subsequent `getToken()` call then permanently falls into the 'wait a bit and use whatever we have' branch, forever returning the same stale `currentToken` (or `null`) — a single failed refresh permanently breaks the client until a full page reload.

The 'someone else is refreshing' branch (`await sleep(50); return currentToken;`) is a single fixed-duration poll, not a loop or a subscription to the in-flight refresh. If the actual `/auth/refresh` round-trip takes longer than 50ms (entirely plausible on a slow network, which is exactly when refreshes matter most), the waiting caller returns before `currentToken` has been updated, handing back an expired/invalid token to its caller and causing the downstream authenticated request to fail with a spurious 401.

Worse than merely 'stale': per the code comment, 'the server invalidates oldToken the moment it receives this request' — so as soon as the refreshing call's POST lands, `currentToken` (still holding the old value) is guaranteed-revoked server-side, not just close to expiry. Any concurrent caller that reads `currentToken` in that window (either via the sleep(50) branch or via the initiating call's own in-flight requests started before refresh) will deterministically get a 401, not just probabilistically.

The waiting branch never re-validates the token it returns — no `isExpired(currentToken)` re-check and no loop back to the top of `getToken()` — so if refresh is still in progress (or has silently failed per the unhandled-rejection bug) after the 50ms sleep, the function unconditionally hands back whatever is in `currentToken`, including `null` on first load or an already-expired value.

No shared 'refresh in flight' promise is exposed — waiters synchronize only via a boolean flag plus blind polling, instead of `await`ing the actual `refreshToken()` promise the first caller kicked off. This is why the retry/staleness bugs above exist: proper coordination would let every concurrent caller await the same resolved value instead of guessing after a fixed delay.

No expiry buffer/skew margin: `isExpired(currentToken)` is checked at the instant `getToken()` is called, but the token is then used later (e.g. attached to a request that's queued or takes time to send). A token that just barely passes the `!isExpired` check can expire before the request it's attached to actually reaches the server, causing intermittent auth failures unrelated to the refresh logic itself.

`currentToken` and `refreshing` are plain module-level variables with no cross-tab coordination (no BroadcastChannel/localStorage/lock). If the user has multiple tabs open, each tab refreshes independently; since the server invalidates the old token immediately on refresh (per the code comment), one tab refreshing will invalidate the token another tab is actively using or about to use, producing exactly the 'intermittent logout, no clear repro from frontend' symptom described in the scenario.

No validation of the refresh response shape: `const newToken = resp.newToken` is used unchecked. If the server ever returns a response without `newToken` (error body with 200 status, malformed response, etc.), `currentToken` becomes `undefined`, which is falsy, so the very next `getToken()` call immediately re-triggers a fresh refresh with no backoff/circuit-breaker — risking a tight retry loop against the refresh endpoint.

Since call sites invoke `getToken()` independently with 'no shared request queue' (per the prose), there is no mechanism to pause or hold in-flight authenticated requests while a refresh is happening and then retry them with the new token; requests that already grabbed the soon-to-be-invalidated token before the refresh started have no retry-on-401 path described, so they simply fail once the old token is revoked.

No timeout/abort on `api.post` inside `refreshToken`: if the refresh request hangs indefinitely (rather than rejecting), `refreshing` stays `true` forever with no failure signal at all, silently wedging every future caller into the stale-return branch — indistinguishable from the unhandled-rejection bug but with no error ever surfacing to logs or callers.
